title: Confounding versus the coefficient
dek: A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome. It is not “any covariate that changed the estimate” and not “anything associated with Y.”
story: Confounding is a causal idea: U affects A and U affects Y, opening a backdoor. Association after “control” is a statistical idea. They meet when your controls are a sufficient adjustment set and your estimator is consistent for the functional the DAG identified.

Lineage confounding a mutation–MIC association is the genomics default. Socioeconomic confounding of a clinic’s apparent treatment effect is the epi default. In both, randomisation of A would have cut A’s incoming arrows from U. Regression is a substitute with a graph attached.

Noncollapsibility: in a logit, the marginal OR and the conditional-on-U OR can differ even without confounding (no arrow from U to A). Changing the coefficient when you add U is therefore not a diagnostic of confounding by itself. Look at the graph and at a collapsible scale (risk difference) if you need that diagnostic.
deepTitle: Difference in coefficients, and what randomisation does
deep: Omitted-variable algebra for OLS is a special case: bias = πγ when U is left out. For GLMs, compare nested scores, but do not treat Δβ as a causal theorem on the log-odds scale.

Measured confounding: put Z in the adjustment set if the DAG says so. Unmeasured confounding: sensitivity analysis, negative controls, or a design (randomisation, instrument, discontinuity). A sandwich SE does not bound unmeasured U.

Table 2 fallacy: reporting every coefficient in a mutually adjusted GLM as if each were a total causal effect. The model that identifies the effect of A given Z may not identify the effect of Z. Caption only the estimand you designed.

In WGS–DST, mixing “confounded by lineage” with “mediated by lineage” is a scientific fork: if lineage is a cause of carrying the mutation, it is a confounder of a total effect of something else, or a competitor. Draw it.

formulas.label: Backdoor sketch
formulas.expression: A ← U → Y   and   A → Y
formulas.note: The U path is confounding. Blocking it (design or adjustment) is the job.

formulas.label: Collapsible contrast (risk difference)
formulas.note: More collapsible than ORs. Still not causal without an assignment assumption.

visual.caption: Confounding as a fork: lineage (or SES, or lab) points to both exposure and outcome. The direct A→Y arrow is the target only after the fork is blocked. A sandwich on the A coefficient does not block U.

example.title: Δβ is not a confounder detector on the OR scale
example.setup: Logit of death on a new drug A. Add HIV. β_A moves from −0.4 to −0.2. A colleague calls HIV a confounder “because the coefficient changed.”

steps.title: Ask the graph
steps.body: Does HIV cause treatment assignment and death? If treatment was randomised, HIV is a precision covariate, not a confounder, even if Δβ is nonzero (noncollapsibility / chance).

steps.title: If observational
steps.body: HIV may well be a confounder. Then adjustment is on the table. Still report a risk difference or standardised means if you want a collapsible contrast.

steps.title: Table 2
steps.body: Do not also publish “the causal effect of HIV” from the same mutually adjusted logit unless that was a second identified estimand.

example.takeaway: Confounding is a fork in a graph. Coefficient change is a clue with false positives on noncollapsible scales.

check.prompt: A confounder of A → Y is best described as:
choices: A common cause (or a proxy for one) that opens a backdoor between A and Y
Any variable that changes β_A when added, on any scale
check.answer: A common cause (or a proxy for one) that opens a backdoor between A and Y
check.why: Causal definition. Association with Y is not enough (mediators, colliders, instruments).

check.prompt: OLS OVB: true β_A = 0, γ_U = 2, π_{U on A} = 0.5. Short-regression coefficient of A is:
check.why: δ = β + πγ = 0 + 0.5×2 = 1. A null causal effect looks like 1 because of the fork.

whyWrong.0: The causal β, not the short coefficient.

check.prompt: On the fork diagram, why do two arrows leave U?
check.figureHint: U points to A and to Y.
choices: Because U is a mediator of A
Because a confounder is a common cause: it must feed both exposure and outcome
check.answer: Because a confounder is a common cause: it must feed both exposure and outcome
check.why: One arrow would be a different motif. Randomisation would delete U → A, not add it.

whyWrong.Because U is a mediator of A: Mediator sits on A → M → Y.
